title: Live from Legal Week 2025: Unveiling a New AI Course for Lawyers — full episode transcript
pub: AI and the Future of Law / 2030 Vision, American Arbitration Association
author: Jen Leonard · Bridget McCormack

st.t: Associate training: Automation threatens expertise reproduction
st.an: The source does not substantively address the cluster’s central apprenticeship and verification paradox. Instead, it reframes the priority around platform-neutral, human-centred change management, active lawyer participation and organisational leadership in AI adoption.

It can give you a sophistication around what change management looks like with a disruption that is a general-purpose technology like this one, and a framework for how to think about it and how to be a leader in a legal organization around change management.

st.t: Dispute resolution: Assistance differs from machine adjudication
st.an: The source advocates professional openness and reinvention in response to AI, loosely aligning with the cluster’s implementation-and-learning theme. However, it does not address the cluster’s central dispute-resolution propositions: expanding access, distinguishing AI assistance from machine adjudication, process legitimacy, safeguards, or the weakness of performance evidence.

st.t: Practitioner engagement: Redesign should precede technological certainty
st.an: The source accepts the cluster’s practitioner-led, implementation-first proposition and materially develops it through a concrete, tool-agnostic leadership course derived from AAA experience. It frames AI adoption as firm-wide change management rather than a technical upgrade, while preserving a client-centred augmentation model. Its support remains chiefly experiential rather than outcome-measured.
qs: The tech is much easier to learn than the change-management piece, I think.

And that project is an online course that law firm leaders or individuals at firms – like, say you're at a firm that's done nothing around AI (which is not uncommon these days) and you'd like to do something – you can take an online course that tracks the roadmap that you and your colleagues have used to transform the way the AAA thinks about its business.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The source accepts that legal AI value depends on organisational redesign rather than tool procurement and materially extends this with a whole-team, learner-centred change model built around practical, context-specific education and safe experimentation. It does not directly assess task-level capability, verification burdens or general legal competence.
qs: (And you've heard me also say this a million times.) I think this is a moment where you absolutely cannot trust the change management to your engineering team, even though it is a tech disruption – it has to be every member of your team, everybody in.
The much more important thing is to have a mindset around experimentation and learning and growth (within safe confines, which we talk about in the course).

st.t: Delivery economics: AI pressures pricing and apprenticeship
st.an: The source supports the synthesis’s claim that organisational absorption, leadership and incentives—not mere access to AI tools—are immediate adoption constraints. It advocates active participation and reshaping legal services, but offers mainly qualitative AAA experience and does not materially address pricing, verification or apprenticeship economics.
qs: So I do think it's this change-management toolkit that's the most important piece of it.
If I were the leader of a firm, this would be priority one: make sure that our future lawyers know that we take this seriously and are reshaping our legal services.

st.t: Justice capacity: AI potential requires deliberate implementation
st.an: The source supports the cluster’s deliberate, human-centered approach to AI in civil-justice work. It acknowledges the high stakes of public-interest matters and favors AI augmentation while preserving direct lawyer–client contact. Its course promotion suggests readiness-building, but it provides no measured evidence of improved access or service outcomes.

kp.k: AI adoption requires organization-wide participation, not isolated technical ownership
kp.d: Leonard describes a 'bystander effect,' attributed to Norah Olson Bluvshtein, in which a firm disengages because an exceptional innovation leader appears to have AI handled. McCormack argues that general-purpose technology instead requires participation across the organization, not delegation to engineers alone. These are practitioner recommendations rather than measured adoption findings.
qs: It's like the firm thinks it's all handled because Nora is on it (or some other fabulous – probably woman – is on it), and then they check out.
I think this is a moment where you absolutely cannot trust the change management to your engineering team, even though it is a tech disruption – it has to be every member of your team, everybody in.
Some of your best ideas are gonna come from people who are not engineers

kp.k: Legal culture and established success obstruct adaptation
kp.d: McCormack presents the AAA's experience as a case of a successful legacy legal organization overcoming innovation barriers. She attributes difficulty partly to established success and partly to lawyers' cultural and normative responsibilities as risk managers and slow movers. The transcript offers her institutional account, not comparative evidence establishing the AAA's performance or the generality of its experience.
qs: I mean, nothing kills innovation like success. The AAA has been very successful for a very long time.
And change management is especially hard in legal (you've heard me say that a million times) for lots of good reasons.
I mean, they're cultural in part, but they're also normative in important ways – like, lawyers are supposed to be the risk managers and the slow movers in the room.

kp.k: Leadership can turn AI anxiety into experimentation
kp.d: Leonard reports that interviews with about a dozen AAA team members revealed initial fear and uncertainty followed by friendly competition to discover and share uses of AI after McCormack encouraged experimentation. She recommends a learning-and-growth mindset within safe confines rather than technological expertise or premium subscriptions. This is a qualitative account from the course-development interviews, without quantified outcomes.
qs: We met with about a dozen of your team members and spent weeks learning what you all were doing over at the AAA
what we got from interviewing your team – it came up again and again – was this idea that at first people were afraid or nervous or unsure how to use it.
they all talked about this friendly competition that emerged.
The much more important thing is to have a mindset around experimentation and learning and growth (within safe confines, which we talk about in the course).

kp.k: AI education should teach change management beyond particular tools
kp.d: The speakers describe an educational framework derived from the AAA's transformation: generative AI and law-firm business models, innovation culture, project selection and piloting, the innovator's dilemma, and leadership coordination. McCormack distinguishes this platform-agnostic approach from the AAA's own use of OpenAI technology within a Microsoft environment, emphasizing human change management rather than product instruction.
qs: It includes everything from a primer on Gen AI and why it matters for law firm business models to how you nourish a culture of innovation, how you select and pilot AI projects, how you solve for the innovator's dilemma, and then how, as a leader, you orchestrate all of this together.
we're building our own point solutions and AI-native products on OpenAI's technology.
We're a Microsoft shop, so that's what we build with – but we are agnostic in this course about what tech platform you should use.
This is about the human part of change management.

kp.k: Practical modular education aims to scale adoption support
kp.d: Leonard describes six online modules of about 30 minutes each, quizzes, and downloadable fillable worksheets designed to help learners adapt the AAA's experience to their own organizations. Both speakers frame this as a way to scale support beyond individual teaching and presentations. Leonard identifies solo and small practices as struggling for lack of guidance; this is her observation, not a survey finding.
qs: It's online, six modules, about 30 minutes each.
And Mariel designed all these great worksheets too – they're downloadable, fillable PDFs.
Your situation is going to be different from Bridget’s and her team's, so how do you adapt this to what you're doing?
solo and small practices are really struggling because there's nobody there to guide them.
The idea of being able to scale it to the legal profession is what I'm interested in.

kp.k: AI strategy may differentiate firms in lawyer recruitment
kp.d: McCormack recommends that law students consider an organization's AI strategy when selecting employers because their careers must remain viable two, five, and ten years ahead. Leonard argues that AI offers firms a rare opportunity to differentiate themselves to future lawyers, while criticizing some activity as 'innovation by press release' and acknowledging that some firms are doing substantive work. These are career and leadership recommendations, not demonstrated recruitment effects.
qs: a lot of firms right now are doing what I call "innovation by press release"
I really think it should matter in your selection of where you go, because you need a career two years from now, and five years from now, and ten years from now.
And this moment just feels like this rare opportunity for firms to differentiate themselves.
make sure that our future lawyers know that we take this seriously and are reshaping our legal services.

kp.k: Innovation capabilities should transfer beyond the current AI disruption
kp.d: McCormack identifies the central lesson from the AAA's preceding two years of AI-related change as building adaptability, creativity, and a bias toward action. She expects these capabilities to help with future disruptions, competitiveness, and practices appreciated by clients and practitioners. These benefits are expressed as expectations and educational aims rather than measured results.
qs: AI is the reason for what we've done over the last two years
I think the most important lesson is one that's going to be transferable to the next disruption
you can really create a culture of innovation and adaptability and creativity and a bias toward action
not just to be competitive vis-à-vis your peers, but actually to build a practice that your clients really appreciate, but also one that you do too.

kp.k: Further workforce and audience-specific education remains prospective
kp.d: McCormack envisages follow-on modules drawing on AAA experiments concerning workforce movement and team rebuilding, alongside courses tailored to in-house teams, courts, and legal aid organizations. She does not disclose the experiments' methods or results, or specify staffing changes. She also argues that flexible formats offer opportunities unavailable within the fixed schedules and credit structures of law-school education.
qs: So I could imagine follow-on modules for great experiments we've been running that have taught us a lot about moving your workforce and rebuilding your teams.
this particular course I think would be really interesting to do for in-house teams, courts, legal aid organizations…
It's hard if you're a tenured member of a faculty at a law school – semesters start in September and end in November, and everything has to be 14 weeks and either two credits or four credits.
I love that we can build whatever, in whatever format, and then distribute it and give it to people in ways that make a lot more sense with the way people need content now.

kp.k: Public-interest AI should augment lawyers' client-facing work
kp.d: Leonard reports skepticism from public-interest lawyers concerned about high-stakes housing and family matters. Her response advocates keeping lawyers with clients while augmenting other work through AI, rather than substituting AI directly for client representation. The discussion proposes targeted education but provides no measured access-to-justice outcomes or detailed safeguards.
qs: I would say a lot of the skepticism I get in presentations comes from public-interest lawyers – understandably
their pushback is sort of that they're dealing with the most precious parts of people's lives (whether that's housing or their family members).
Because it's precisely those kinds of situations where we want you to be with your clients, and we want all the rest to sort of be augmented through AI, right?

kp.k: Pandemic court adaptation supplies an analogy for educational change
kp.d: McCormack uses pandemic-driven court changes as an analogy for innovation under institutional stress: disruption prompted courts to reach users in ways better suited to their work and family lives and enabled further experimentation. She expects education to benefit similarly from necessary experimentation; Leonard hopes institutional stress will make audiences more receptive to new educational models. These are retrospective practitioner interpretation and prospective analogy, not evidence of AI-driven court outcomes.
qs: it took a significant disruption for courts to figure out that we could reach our users much more effectively in a way that made more sense for them and their jobs and their families.
And then that allowed us to try a whole bunch of new things.
And I do feel like education will benefit from some of this experimentation and innovation that's going to be needed, given the rocky road ahead.

kp.k: General-purpose model comparisons are experiential, not legal benchmarks
kp.d: McCormack reports preferring ChatGPT 4.5 increasingly for creative writing and values combining writing with Deep Research in one platform, while both speakers describe comparing outputs across models. Leonard sometimes combines outputs through another model. Their comments about Claude's new internet connectivity and relative competitiveness are provisional personal assessments; Leonard explicitly identifies few immediate implications for lawyers beyond their own information-gathering use.
qs: I've just found 4.5 to be a little better, a more creative writer than the earlier versions were.
I like to do the same thing in a few different models just to see how they all do.
sometimes I'll take the results and plug them both into one model and ask it to orchestrate them – or harmonize them, I should say.
Not a ton of implications for lawyers yet, other than the continued sort of supremacy of Deep Research in our lives for getting information.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: McCormack and Leonard argue that AI requires organisation-wide change rather than a technology upgrade delegated to specialists.
pts.d: McCormack characterises AI as a general-purpose disruption whose adoption requires participation from the whole team, including non-engineers. Leonard argues that leadership, experimentation and learning matter more than technical expertise or access to the leading subscription. These are prescriptions grounded in their account of the AAA's transformation, not quantified findings about adoption outcomes.

pts.k: McCormack says AI can help lawyers solve longstanding problems, while Leonard proposes augmentation that preserves public-interest lawyers' time with clients.
pts.d: McCormack expresses conditional optimism about lawyers working with AI as a teammate; she does not specify the longstanding problems or quantify their resolution. Leonard specifically envisages AI augmenting work surrounding direct client engagement in sensitive public-interest matters, rather than replacing lawyers in those relationships. Her statement is an aspiration for service delivery, not a report of demonstrated client outcomes.

pts.k: Leonard predicts that credible AI strategies can differentiate firms and attract lawyers; McCormack says those strategies should influence career choices.
pts.d: Leonard contrasts firms' historical similarity with an emerging opportunity to distinguish themselves by visibly reshaping legal services and engaging staff in AI learning. McCormack independently endorses assessing prospective employers' technology strategies for longer-term career prospects. Neither speaker presents recruitment data or claims a measured employment effect.

pts.k: McCormack claims that AI-driven organisational learning can improve competitiveness and practice quality while preparing lawyers for subsequent disruptions.
pts.d: She argues that developing innovation, adaptability, creativity and a bias toward action can create practices valued by clients and practitioners, with benefits transferable beyond AI. Leonard reports that AAA staff moved from uncertainty toward active experimentation and friendly competition after leadership encouraged new possibilities. The claimed benefits are qualitative and prospective.

pts.k: The speakers present modular online education as a way to scale AI change-management support across the profession, with further audience-specific courses possible.
pts.d: Leonard describes an already-launched, six-module course translating the AAA's experience into adaptable tools for firms and individuals. McCormack envisages follow-on modules on workforce and team changes and versions for in-house teams, courts and legal aid organisations. She also predicts improvements to the business and operations of law in the coming years, but does not detail or measure those improvements. Future courses are possibilities, not completed deployments.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The principal evidence is the speakers' own organisational experience, interviews with AAA staff and encounters with legal audiences.
pts.d: Leonard says her team interviewed about a dozen AAA team members over several weeks to construct the curriculum. McCormack describes the AAA's experience overcoming legacy-organisational barriers and building AI products. Leonard cites a recent Philadelphia Bar Association visit when describing solo and small-practice difficulties. These are qualitative accounts supplied by the course's creators and organisational participants; the transcript provides no controlled comparisons, productivity measurements, client-outcome data or benchmark results. The broad forecasts about competitiveness, recruitment and better legal services are not accompanied by separate empirical tests.

pts.k: Reported third-party signals support demand for AI literacy and education, rather than demonstrating legal-service improvements.
pts.d: Leonard attributes a rising-skills ranking to LinkedIn. McCormack relays PLI CEO Sharon Crane's report of demand for AI content. These remain attributed reports: no underlying dataset, methodology or demand figures appear in the transcript. They support the speakers' rationale for educational provision, not the predicted performance or recruitment benefits.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The account concerns current adoption in 2025, approximately two years of AAA experimentation, and an unspecified future transformation.
pts.d: The course is announced at LegalWeek 2025. McCormack refers to AI motivating the AAA's work over the preceding two years; her career advice explicitly looks two, five and ten years ahead. Wider improvements are expected 'in the coming years' without milestones. Conditions include broad staff participation, committed leadership, safe experimentation and adaptation to the learner's organisation. McCormack identifies successful incumbency, legal culture and lawyers' risk-management responsibilities as barriers. Additional educational innovation is conditional on organisational capacity and flexibility.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claims span firm leaders and staff, prospective recruits, smaller practices, legal-service clients and potential institutional learners.
pts.d: Firm leaders are expected to organise AI adoption rather than leave it to engineers or a single innovation leader; non-engineering staff are potential sources of ideas. Individual lawyers and students may use AI literacy and change-management knowledge in career decisions. Solo and small practices are described as lacking guidance. Clients may benefit from more responsive practices, and public-interest clients from lawyers retaining direct engagement while AI augments surrounding work. In-house teams, courts and legal aid organisations are proposed audiences for future educational adaptations, not documented beneficiaries of the current course.
